paragraphs.en: As a historian who’s always searching for the text or the image that makes us re-evaluate the past,I’ve become preoccupied with looking for photographs that show our Victorian ancestors smiling ( what better way to shatter the image of 19th-century prudery?). I’ve found quite a few, and—since I started posting them on Twitter—they have been causing quite a stir. People have been surprised to see evidence that Victorians had fun and could,and did, laugh. They are noting that the Victorians suddenly seem to become more human as the hundred-or-so years that separate us fade away through our common experience of laughter.
paragraphs.zh: 作为一名总在寻找能够让我们重新审视过去的文字或图像的历史学家，我最近一直热衷于寻找维多利亚时代祖辈们面带笑容的照片——还有什么比这更能打破19世纪人们拘谨刻板的形象呢？我已经找到了不少，而自从我开始把它们发布到推特上之后，这些照片引起了不小的轰动。人们惊讶地看到，维多利亚时代的人也会寻欢作乐，也能笑，而且确实笑过。他们注意到，当共同的欢笑体验使相隔的一百多年岁月逐渐淡去时，维多利亚时代的人突然显得更有人情味了。

paragraphs.en: Of course, I need to concede that my collection of ‘Smiling Victorians’ makes up only a tiny percentage of the vast catalogue of photographic portraiture created between 1840 and 1900, the majority of which show sitters posing miserably and stiffly in front of painted backdrops, or staring absently into the middle distance.How do we explain this trend?
paragraphs.zh: 当然，我需要承认，我收集的这些“微笑的维多利亚人”照片，在1840年至1900年间数量庞大的人像摄影作品中只占极小比例。那些照片中的人物大多在绘制的背景幕前愁容满面、僵硬地摆着姿势，或心不在焉地望向不远处。我们该如何解释这种倾向？

paragraphs.en: During the 1840s and 1850s, in the early days of photography, exposure times were notoriously long: the daguerreotype photographic method (producing an image on a silvered copper plate) could take several minutes to complete, resulting in blurred images as sitters shifted position or adjusted their limbs. The thought of holding a fixed grin as the camera performed its magical duties was too much to contemplate, and so anon-committal blank stare became the norm.
paragraphs.zh: 19世纪40至50年代，也就是摄影术的早期，曝光时间长得出了名：银版摄影法，即在镀银铜板上成像的方法，可能需要几分钟才能完成，拍摄对象一旦移动身体或调整四肢的位置，图像就会变得模糊。一想到要在相机施展其神奇功能时始终咧嘴微笑，人们就觉得难以忍受，因此，毫无表情、茫然直视便成了常态。

paragraphs.en: But exposure times were much quicker by the 1880s, and the introduction of the Box Brownie and other portable cameras meant that, though slow by today’s digital standards, the exposure was almost instantaneous.Spontaneous smiles were relatively easy to capture by the 1890s, so we must look elsewhere for an explanation of why Victorians still hesitated to smile.
paragraphs.zh: 但到19世纪80年代，曝光速度已经快了许多；布朗尼盒式相机和其他便携相机的问世，意味着尽管按今天的数码标准来看还不够快，曝光却几乎可以在瞬间完成。到了19世纪90年代，捕捉自然流露的微笑已经相对容易，因此，我们必须从其他方面寻找解释：为何维多利亚时代的人仍然不愿微笑？

paragraphs.en: One explanation might be the loss of dignity displayed through a cheesy grin. “Nature gave us lips to conceal our teeth,” ran one popular Victorian maxim, alluding to the fact that before the birth of proper dentistry, mouths were often in a shocking state of hygiene. A flashing set of healthy and clean, regular ‘pearly whites’ was a rare sight in Victorian society, the preserve of the super-rich (and even then,dental hygiene was not guaranteed).
paragraphs.zh: 一种解释可能是，咧嘴大笑显得有失体面。维多利亚时代一句流行的格言说：“大自然赐予我们嘴唇，是为了遮住牙齿。”这暗示了一个事实：在正规牙科诞生之前，人们的口腔卫生状况往往糟糕得令人震惊。在维多利亚时代的社会里，能亮出一口健康、洁净、整齐、珍珠般洁白牙齿的人极为罕见，只有超级富豪才可能做到——即便是他们，牙齿卫生也并非有保障。

paragraphs.en: A toothy grin ( especially when there were gaps or blackened gnashers) lacked class: drunks,tramps,and music hall performers might gurn and grin with a smile as wide as Lewis Carroll’s gum-exposing Cheshire Cat, but it was not a becoming look for properly bred persons. Even Mark Twain, a man who enjoyed a hearty laugh, said that when it came to photographic portraits there could be “nothing more damning than a silly, foolish smile fixed forever”.
paragraphs.zh: 露齿大笑，尤其在牙齿有缺口或发黑的情况下，显得缺乏格调：醉汉、流浪汉和歌舞厅演员也许会挤眉弄眼、咧嘴大笑，笑得像刘易斯·卡罗尔笔下那只露着牙龈的柴郡猫一样夸张，但这种模样不适合有教养的人。就连喜欢开怀大笑的马克·吐温也说，谈到人像摄影，“没有什么比一副被永远定格的傻乎乎、蠢兮兮的笑容更糟糕了”。
